## Introduction

- Lymphadenectomy extent during esophagectomy remains **controversial**
- Esophageal cancer often presents with **local nodal and distant metastases**
- Locally advanced disease typically treated with **neoadjuvant modalities**
- Central debate:
  - Radical dissection improves **locoregional control** and survival
  - Extended dissection improves **staging accuracy**, counseling, and adjuvant therapy decisions

---

## Lymphatic Drainage of the Esophagus {.smaller}

- Esophagus traverses **three body compartments**
- Lymph flow occurs in a **wide pattern of spread**
- Embryological origins:
  - **Above**: branchial arches and pharyngeal pouches
  - **Below**: splanchnic mesoderm
- Join during development but remain demarcated at the **tracheal bifurcation**
  - Leads to **bilateral lymphatic drainage** (Fig. 34.1)

---

## Patterns of Lymphatic Spread {.smaller}

**Early esophageal cancer:**

- Nodal spread follows **anatomical pathways**
- **Tumor location determines** likely node involvement
  - **Above tracheal bifurcation** → upper mediastinum and neck
  - **Below bifurcation** → celiac axis
  - **At bifurcation** → either direction
- **Skipping of stations is rare** in early tumors

**Histology differences (T1a-M3):**

- **SCC**: up to **12%** lymph node involvement
- **Adenocarcinoma**: only **1.3%**

---

## Submucosal Spread and Advanced Disease

- **Extensive submucosal lymphatic network** allows longitudinal communication between proximal and distal drainage systems
- In advanced tumors blocking primary pathways:
  - Submucosal system allows **eccentric lymph node involvement**
- Most patients diagnosed at **advanced stage**
- **T3 disease**: up to **85%** chance of lymph node metastasis

---

## Lymph Node Tiers and Fields

- Extent of dissection divided into **three fields**:
  1. **Upper abdomen**
  2. **Mediastinum**
  3. **Neck** (Fig. 34.2)

- **Three-field dissection**: nodal tissue from all three areas
- **Two-field dissection**: definition varies by geography and histology prevalence

---

## Two-Field Dissection: East vs West {.smaller}

| Region | Common Histology | Two-Field Definition |
|--------|------------------|----------------------|
| **Japan/East** | Squamous Cell Carcinoma | Upper abdomen + inferior and superior mediastinum + both recurrent laryngeal nerves |
| **Western countries** | Adenocarcinoma | Upper abdomen + inferior mediastinum only (to level of carina) |

- Western definition reflects tumors located in **lower esophagus or EGJ**

---

## Abdominal Lymph Node Dissection (Field 1) {.smaller}

**Node stations included:**

- **Superior gastric group**
  - Paracardial nodes (left and right = single group)
  - Lesser curve nodes
  - Nodes along left gastric artery
- **Celiac trunk nodes** (at root of left gastric, common hepatic, splenic arteries)
- **Common hepatic nodes**

*Remove en bloc with primary lesion. Disease beyond celiac or hepatic nodes = metastatic disease.*

---

## Abdominal Involvement Patterns

- **Paracardial and lesser curve regions** most commonly involved with lower esophageal tumors
- Left gastric, celiac trunk, and hepatic artery nodes frequently involved
- **Intramural spread** to abdominal nodes:
  - **Adenocarcinoma**: **54%**
  - **SCC**: **10%**
- Indicates need for **wide resection margin** in adenocarcinoma patients

---

## Thoracic Lymph Node Dissection (Field 2) {.smaller}

**Standard mediastinal dissection includes:**

- Mediastinal nodes
- Thoracic duct
- Both pulmonary hilar nodes
- Paraesophageal nodes
- Carinal, bronchial, and paratracheal nodes

*Taken as en bloc resection with esophagus*

**Extended dissection:**

- Nodes on **right side of trachea**

**Total mediastinal lymphadenectomy:**

- Additional removal along **left recurrent laryngeal nerve** and **subaortic nodes**

---

## Cervical Node Dissection (Field 3) {.smaller}

**Three-field dissection adds:**

- Brachiocephalic nodes
- Deep internal cervical nodes
- Deep external cervical nodes
- Nodes along **left and right recurrent laryngeal nerves**

**Involvement patterns:**

- Deep external (lateral to IJV) and deep internal (approximate RLN) **more commonly involved**
- Deep lateral nodes (spinal accessory chain) **less commonly involved**

---

## SCC vs Adenocarcinoma: Overview

- Pattern of spread correlates **somewhat with histology**
- Extensive lymphatic drainage makes prediction difficult, especially in **advanced cancers**
- **Figs. 34.3 and 34.4** illustrate different distribution patterns

---

## SCC: Nodal Involvement Rates

- Typically located in **middle and proximal esophagus**
- **Confined to mucosa**: 0–7% nodal involvement
- **Submucosal invasion**: up to **50%** nodal involvement
- **Transmural tumors**: over **73%** nodal involvement

---

## SCC: Recurrence Patterns {.smaller}

**Law et al. (n=108, SCC, two-field):**

- Two-thirds recur in **first year**
- Majority (**44**) **extrathoracic**
  - 28 distant organs (hematogenous)
  - 17 lymph nodes (12 cervical, 5 abdominal)
- **Local recurrence**: **25%**

---

## Adenocarcinoma: Nodal Involvement

- Typically **lower esophagus and EGJ**
- **Confined to mucosa**: 0–7% (mirrors SCC)
- **Submucosal penetration**: 15–50%
- **Muscularis propria invasion**: up to **80%**

---

## Adenocarcinoma: Recurrence Rates

- Lower esophageal adenocarcinoma: **9%** local recurrence
- Junctional cancers: **15%** local recurrence
- Overall local recurrence either subtype: **25–50%**
- Meticulous lymphadenectomy may have **profound impact** on locoregional control

---

## Figure 34.3: SCC Nodal Distribution

Distribution of lymph node metastases in **100 SCC patients**:

| Region | Involvement |
|--------|-------------|
| Cervical/Neck | 11.2% |
| Upper Mediastinum | 31.9% |
| Carina/Tracheal bifurcation | 56.6% |
| Lower Mediastinum | 30.2% |
| Paraesophageal (mid-lower) | 20.9% |
| Gastroesophageal/Paracardial | 22.6% |
| Left Gastric | 12.3% |
| Celiac Axis | 8.2% |

---

## Figure 34.4: Adenocarcinoma Nodal Distribution

Distribution of lymph node metastases in **100 adenocarcinoma patients**:

| Region | Involvement |
|--------|-------------|
| Cervical | 5.4% |
| Upper Mediastinum | 9.7% |
| Lower Mediastinum | 31.5% |
| Paracardial/EGJ | 43.9% |
| Left Gastric/Celiac area | 50.6% |
| Additional abdominal stations | 12.8% |
| Hepatic/Common hepatic | 10.2% |

---

## Figure 34.2: Fields of Dissection

**Three anatomical fields routinely dissected:**

1. **Abdominal field** (one-field)
   - Celiac axis, paracardial, lesser curve, left gastric artery

2. **Thoracic field** (two-field)
   - Mediastinal nodes from diaphragm to subaortic region
   - Paraesophageal, hilar, carinal, paratracheal

3. **Cervical field** (three-field)
   - Deep internal, external, and lateral cervical nodes
   - Recurrent laryngeal nerve chains

---

## Box 34.1: Nodes by Anatomic Region {.smaller}

| Region | Node Stations |
|--------|---------------|
| **Cervical** | Deep lateral, Deep external, Deep internal |
| **Superior Mediastinal** | Recurrent nerve chain, Paratracheal, Brachiocephalic artery, Infraaortic-arch |
| **Middle Mediastinal** | Tracheal bifurcation, Pulmonary hilar, Paraesophageal |
| **Lower Mediastinal** | Paraesophageal, Diaphragmatic |
| **Superior Gastric** | Paracardial, Lesser curve, Left gastric artery |
| **Celiac Trunk** | Celiac axis nodes |
| **Common Hepatic** | Common hepatic artery nodes |

---

## Kurokawa Nodal Categories (EGJ Tumors) {.smaller}

Mapped lymph node involvement comparing adenocarcinoma vs SCC:

**Category 1: Strongly recommended (>10% involvement)**

- Abdominal stations: **1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 11p**
- Lower mediastinal **110** if >2 cm esophageal involvement

**Category 2: Weakly recommended (5–10%)**

- Abdominal stations: **8a, 19**
- Lower mediastinal **110** (if ≤2 cm involvement)

**Category 3: Not recommended (<5%)**

- All other stations

---

## Implications of Lymphadenectomy {.smaller}

**Core arguments for extensive dissection:**

1. Improved **locoregional control** and cure rates
2. Improved **staging accuracy**
3. Better **patient counseling**
4. Informed **adjuvant therapy** decisions

**Key principle:**

- **R0 resection** is critical prognostic indicator
- **R1/R2 residual disease** → significantly worse prognosis
- **25–50%** develop locoregional recurrence after two-field dissection

---

## Survival and Nodal Location {.smaller}

**Anderegg et al. (n=479, adenocarcinoma):**

- Nodal involvement location = **independent predictor**
- Survival by location:
  - **Locoregional only**: 35 months
  - **Celiac trunk nodes**: 16 months
  - **Proximal field nodes**: 15 months

**Hulscher et al.:**

- Trend toward greater **5-year survival** with transthoracic + extended en bloc vs. transhiatal for lower esophageal/junctional adenocarcinoma

---

## Node Yield as Surrogate for Extent {.smaller}

| Study | Design | Findings |
|-------|--------|----------|
| **Van der Schaaf** | Swedish nationwide, n=1044 | More extensive clearance **did not** equate to improved survival. Low yields (3rd quartile ≤15 nodes) |
| **Lagergren** | Single center | Higher yield **did not** equate to better survival. 3rd quartile ≤20 nodes |
| **Visser et al.** | Meta-analysis | Higher LN yield **associated with improved survival** in both neoadjuvant-naive and modern cohorts |

*Note: Both early studies had generally low lymph node yields*

---

## Lymph Node Ratio (LNR) {.smaller}

- **LNR** = positive nodes / total nodes examined
- Better predictor than N category alone?

**Chen et al. (n>2000, SCC, China):**

- Proposed **Nr categories**:
  - **0**: 61% survival
  - **0–10%**: 41% survival
  - **10–20%**: 33% survival
  - **>20%**: 23% survival

**Bhamidipati et al. (n=347, US, predominantly adenocarcinoma):**

- LNR = **independent predictor** of prognosis
- More useful than N category alone

---

## Micrometastases

- Present in up to **50%** of N0 patients
- May explain recurrence in node-negative patients
- Prognostic significance debated:
  - Some: immunohistochemically detected deposits = poorer prognosis
  - Others: no prognostic consequence

---

## Tailoring Lymphadenectomy

- Ideal to tailor by stage, but accurate assessment of involved nodes remains **difficult**
- Sentinel node techniques attempted
- **Skip metastases** and unpredictability make sentinel approach **currently unreliable**
- Tailoring so that only metastatic nodes are removed is **fraught with high false-negative rates**

---

## Optimal Node Yield and Systemic Disease {.smaller}

**Phillips et al. (adenocarcinoma, post-neoadjuvant):**

- **23% decrease in survival** had no formal lymphadenectomy been performed
- Leaving **abdominal nodes behind** = minimal impact in lower esophageal/junctional adenocarcinoma

**Peyre et al. (n=1053, no neoadjuvant):**

- Systemic disease probability:
  - **>50%** when >3 nodes involved
  - **Approaches 100%** when >8 nodes involved

**Peyre et al. (n=2303):**

- Optimum threshold: **23 nodes**
- **Location matters**, not just number

---

## Extended Resection Indications

**Omloo et al.:**

- Extended resection beneficial in patients with **<8 lymph node metastases**
- Given difficulty identifying these patients preoperatively → **complete two-field lymphadenectomy** in all patients where nodal involvement is a concern

**Rizk et al.:**

- Optimum yield depends on **T category**
- Recommend **31–42 nodes** in T3 disease or worse

---

## Three-Field Lymphadenectomy: Background

- **Longstanding debate**
- **Widely employed in Japan** for many years
- **Relatively infrequent in the West**
- Concerns:
  - Increased **morbidity and mortality** with cervical dissection
  - Argument that nodal involvement = **systemic disease**, no survival advantage

---

## Three-Field: Evidence from Lerut et al. {.smaller}

**Long-term outcomes (unimodality treatment era):**

| Tumor Type | Cervical Nodes+ | 5-Year Survival |
|------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| GEJ adenocarcinoma | Yes | **0%** |
| Distal-third adenocarcinoma | Yes | **12%** |
| Middle-third SCC | Yes | **28%** |

**Key findings:**

- **25%** of patients had cervical LN involvement
- **75%** of these **not detected** on initial staging
- 4-year survival distal adenocarcinoma = **36%** (possible palliative role)
- RLN damage: only **2.6%**
- **No significant increase** in overall complications

---

## Three-Field in Squamous Cell Carcinoma {.smaller}

- Japanese studies: almost **1/3 of SCC patients** have cervical node involvement
- **Chen et al. (n=1715, SCC):**
  - Cervical node involvement increases with more **proximal** tumors:
    - Proximal third: **44%**
    - **Lower third: 23%** (strikingly high)
- Multiple systematic reviews in predominantly squamous populations:
  - **Superior survival** with three-field vs. two-field dissection

**Conclusion:** Strong rationale for three-field in SCC

---

## Three-Field in Adenocarcinoma {.smaller}

- **Paucity of data**, especially in neoadjuvant era
- Lerut data showed **poor overall survival** for adenocarcinoma with cervical involvement
- **Routine cervical dissection may not be merited** for adenocarcinoma

**When to consider:**

- Adenocarcinoma with **extensive mediastinal nodal disease**
- Decision based on:
  - Extent of disease
  - Likelihood of recurrence
  - Overall fitness

**Authors' practice:** Multidisciplinary discussion; individualized patient counseling

---

## Morbidity of Lymphadenectomy: Overview

- Extended lymphadenectomy associated by some with **increased morbidity**
- **Transhiatal** esophagectomy: fewer complications than **transthoracic** with extended en bloc dissection
- Main problems: **respiratory complications**
  - Pneumonia
  - Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

---

## Specific Surgical Risks {.smaller}


::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
**Tracheobronchial tree:**

- Risk of **direct injury** during extensive dissection
- **Delayed injury** from inadvertent cautery use

**Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN):**

- Risk increased with more extensive dissection

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
**Thoracic duct:**

- Risk of **chyle leak**

**Physiological impact:**

- One-lung ventilation increases capillary permeability → pulmonary edema
- Mediastinal lymphadenectomy **impairs lymphatic flow** → compounds edema

:::
:::



---

## Quality of Life and Volume Outcomes {.smaller}

**Schandl et al. (Swedish nationwide):**

- **No association** between number of lymph nodes removed and quality of life at **6 months or 5 years**

**Henckens et al. (Dutch high-volume unit):**

- High lymph node yields **achievable without increasing complication rates**
- **>31 nodes removed** associated with improved survival
- Supports centralization to **high-volume centers**

---

## RAMIE and Modern Considerations {.smaller}

**van der Horst et al. (Robot-Assisted MIE):**

- **50%** major complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥3b)
- Most common: **RLN palsy** and **pneumonia**
- Only **5%** unexpected contralateral lymph node metastasis

**Implication:**

- Even with modern technology, **high morbidity** exists
- Questionable oncological benefit for extensive dissection in some patients
- Need for careful **patient selection**

---

## Summary: Staging and Adjuvant Therapy {.smaller}

**AJCC 8th Edition (2018):**

- N category grouped by **number of positive nodes**
- **Does not specify** adequate lymph node yield for accurate staging
- Inadequate yield risks **understaging and stage migration**

**Adjuvant therapy:**

- Increasing evidence for adjuvant treatment post-esophagectomy
- Recent meta-analysis: improved survival at **1 year**, sustained to **5 years**
- Adequate lymphadenectomy identifies patients who benefit from **further treatment**

---

## Summary: Final Recommendations {.smaller}

1. **SCC and adenocarcinoma are distinct entities** — future studies must analyze separately
2. Leaving positive nodes behind likely **hastens recurrence**
3. **Neoadjuvant therapy** may sterilize residual disease in some patients, but this is **unpredictable**
4. Authors advocate **unequivocal en bloc resection** with comprehensive lymphadenectomy
5. Extent should be tailored to:
   - **Histology** (three-field for SCC; selective for adenocarcinoma)
   - **Tumor location**
   - **Patient fitness**
   - **Multidisciplinary assessment**

---

**Key Takeaway**

> A meticulous, anatomy-driven lymphadenectomy remains essential for optimal staging, locoregional control, and survival in esophageal cancer surgery.
